summary: This document defines a YANG data model to configure and manage Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD). The modules conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).

plainLanguage.summary: BFD quickly notices if a link between two routers stops working. This document defines a standard form to set it up and see how it is doing.

questions: what is the yang data model for bfd
what bfd path types does yang support
how is a bfd session identified in yang
subtitle: A set of YANG modules for configuring and monitoring BFD sessions on IP, MPLS and LAG paths.

tldr.problem: BFD detects liveness of many kinds of forwarding paths, but there was no standard data model to configure BFD or read its state, and no single key identifies a BFD session across path types.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a family of NMDA-conformant YANG modules: shared types, a common bfd container, and one module each for IP single-hop, IP multihop, LAG and MPLS LSPs.
tldr.outcome: Operators and tools get a common way to configure sessions, read per-session state and statistics, and receive notifications. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9314.

facts.label: Path types
facts.value: IP single-hop, IP multihop, MPLS LSP, LAG

today: RFC 9127 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9314. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the Model Covers
sections.content:
This document defines a YANG data model to configure and manage Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD), a protocol for liveness detection of arbitrary paths between systems. It covers BFD over single-hop IP, multihop IP, MPLS Label Switched Paths and Link Aggregation Groups. BFD over pseudowires (VCCV) is not addressed.

BFD usually does not run alone. Control protocols called BFD clients, such as static routes or routing protocols whose hellos cannot detect failure in under a second (OSPF and IS-IS), use its services.

The modules conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA, RFC 8342), so there are no separate top-level containers for configuration and operational state.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD is a tiny, fast check that asks a neighbor 'are you still there?' This document says how to write down the settings for those checks in a form every vendor understands.

sections.title: One Module per Path Type
sections.content:
Because BFD checks many kinds of forwarding paths, no uniform key identifies a session. The model therefore splits into several modules, one per path type; they differ mainly in the key of the list holding the sessions. Common types and groupings avoid duplication.

A new control-plane protocol, bfdv1, is defined, with a bfd container under control-plane-protocol from RFC 8349. Four modules augment it: ietf-bfd-ip-sh adds ip-sh, ietf-bfd-ip-mh adds ip-mh, ietf-bfd-lag adds lag and ietf-bfd-mpls adds mpls.

BFD can run at the network device level, in logical network elements, or in network instances. At device level the model is used as is; otherwise it augments the mounted routing model.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one binder, and each kind of link gets its own tab in it. The tabs look alike but are filed differently.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
The configuration is mostly the parameters of RFC 5880: local-multiplier, desired-min-tx-interval and required-min-rx-interval. Implementations may offer one interval for both directions, so the model offers a choice between min-interval and the separate transmit and receive intervals.

For authentication there is a key-chain reference to the key chain model of RFC 8177, and meticulous to enable meticulous mode.

Per path type, sessions are keyed differently. Single-hop IP uses the interface and destination address pair. Multihop IP uses a session-group keyed by source and destination address, with tx-ttl and rx-ttl for the outgoing and minimum incoming TTL. MPLS sessions are identified by an IP prefix, and there is no LSP configuration on the egress node. LAG configuration is a list of LAGs, with the destination address of the micro-BFD sessions set per LAG and per address family.

A grouping, client-cfg-parms, lets BFD clients that auto-discover peers, such as IGPs, hold their own BFD interval and multiplier settings and create or remove sessions as peers come and go.
sections.plainLanguage: The main dials are how often to check, how many missed checks before calling it broken, and an optional secret password. Different kinds of links are named in different ways.

sections.title: Operational State and Notifications
sections.content:
The operational model holds overall statistics, such as the number of sessions and how many are up, globally under bfd and per forwarding-path type. For each session it exposes three kinds of data: fundamental information (local and remote discriminators, Demand mode support), session-running data (remote state, diagnostic codes, actual transmit and receive intervals) and session-statistics (when the session went up or down, packet counters).

For IP multihop and MPLS, several sessions may test different ECMP paths to one destination, so they appear as multiple sessions inside each session-group.

Notifications tell users about important events, giving the discriminators, the new state, the time in the previous state and the reason for the change. They are defined per path type with common groupings. The model defines no RPC operations. The start and stop of the Echo function is implementation specific, and the appendix shows an example module that adds Echo intervals through configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides the settings, you get a dashboard: how many checks are running, which are healthy, and a message when one changes.

sections.title: Interaction with Other YANG Modules
sections.content:
BFD behavior depends on settings in other models. If enabled in ietf-interfaces is false, no BFD packets can be sent or received on that interface. The IPv4 and IPv6 enabled and forwarding settings in ietf-ip similarly stop BFD IPv4 or IPv6 packets, and mpls-enabled in ietf-mpls does so for BFD MPLS packets.

RFC 8532 describes how the LIME connectionless OAM model could be extended to support BFD.
sections.plainLanguage: If the master switch for a link is off, the checks on it cannot send or hear anything either.

sections.title: Configuration Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives NETCONF XML examples for each path type. The IP single-hop example sets both the desired transmit interval and the required receive interval to 10 ms on interface eth0, with destination 2001:db8:0:113::101. The multihop example sets both intervals to 150 ms for a session group.

There are also examples for a LAG and for MPLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are filled-in forms showing what a real setup looks like.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The modules are accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH and TLS, with NACM (RFC 8341) restricting access. Writable data nodes can be sensitive: the interval and multiplier nodes affect the session, and the address nodes source-addr and dest-addr (and ipv4-dest-addr and ipv6-dest-addr for LAG) can be used to send BFD packets to unwitting recipients. RFC 5880 describes how BFD mitigates such threats. The authentication nodes key-chain and meticulous affect session security.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should be allowed to change the settings, because a wrong change could make a router send checks to the wrong place.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA registered seven XML namespace URIs and seven YANG module names, including iana-bfd-types, ietf-bfd-types, ietf-bfd, ietf-bfd-ip-sh, ietf-bfd-ip-mh, ietf-bfd-lag and ietf-bfd-mpls.

The iana-bfd-types module is IANA-maintained. It mirrors the BFD Diagnostic Codes and BFD Authentication Types registries, and IANA must update it whenever those registries change.
sections.plainLanguage: The official name list now includes these seven modules, and one of them is kept up to date by the registry office.
